Encore une fois, un service destiné aux: Once again, a service for non-francophones, mainly immigrants, has been cut!
Au Moyen Âge, une époque où peu de gens: In the Middle Ages, when few people could read and write, the public writer drafted documents for a fee for those who needed them. Today, the profession still exists, and it is an especially valuable service for newcomers to Quebec, who often face challenges like the language barrier, job hunting, and access to health care and housing.
En rédigeant mon dernier reportage sur l: While writing my last report on the budget cuts affecting immigration services, I thought the public writer service could be an ideal solution for these newcomers, who are so often left without support in Quebec. But to my great surprise, funding for this pilot project has been cut off too.
J’ai rencontré trois personnes aux profi: I met three people with different profiles: a former public writer employed by an organization, a volunteer public writer working from home, and a volunteer at a library. They all agree that this service is essential for newcomers, whether for administrative procedures or for more personal needs. As this service gradually disappears, I wonder where these people will turn for support.
Je vous invite à découvrir comment ce se: I invite you to discover how this service makes a difference for those who need it, before it disappears completely!
<strong>En mars dernier, le projet pilot: Last March, the public writer pilot project came to an end in Quebec. Yet demand remains strong, especially among immigrants who struggle to integrate, in particular because of their difficulty mastering French. Was this service essential to newcomers’ adjustment?
<strong>« Il faut les aider dans l’imméd: “We have to help them right away”
À l’angle du boulevard Crémazie et de la: At a café on the corner of Crémazie Boulevard and Lajeunesse Street, we meet Michel Huot, a former public writer employed by the organization Accueil aux immigrants de l’est de Montréal (AIEM), now a project manager there. In a denim shirt, with a pen in his pocket and a tablet at the ready, the retiree radiates boundless energy.
De 2022 à 2024, il a été au cœur du proj: From 2022 to 2024, he was at the heart of the public writer pilot project, funded by the Ministry of the French Language through the Regroupement des organismes en francisation du Québec (ROFQ), before it was suspended. His role was essential, especially for people overwhelmed by administrative challenges. “Once newcomers are settled in, they run into the real music: a landlord who wants to raise the rent by an exorbitant amount, a first tax return, incomprehensible letters from the government,” he lists, with the precision of a conductor. “So that’s where the public writer comes in.”
De son sac à dos, il sort un document :: From his backpack, he pulls out a document: a printed screenshot of his list of files, a snapshot of the many lives he has touched. “Last year, I met around 350 people, and that was only by being available once a week.” Every Friday, from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Michel Huot met dozens of people in his office at AIEM, in 30-minute appointments. “The goal, at that point, was to understand what the need was. Then, on Mondays, I followed up on files and closed requests,” he explains, before adding: “These people have an emergency, and you can’t tell them, ‘I only work on Fridays, we’ll meet again next week for the follow-up.’ No. We have to help them right away.”
De son stylo, il pointe un dossier. « J’: With his pen, he points to a file. “I wrote a lot of invitation letters for immigrants who wanted to bring their relatives to the country for special events, but also housing application letters.” These letters, along with other administrative documents, are essential to help them settle in.
Bien que les documents rédigés par un éc: Although documents written by a public writer are not legal documents like those signed by a lawyer, they nonetheless carry some weight and credibility, Michel Huot insists. “The fact that a public writer represents an organization like AIEM, which is recognized in the immigration network and by embassies, brings additional recognition, and at no cost.”
Les yeux de nouveau rivés sur son docume: His eyes back on his document, he continues: “I remember one case where a man was desperately looking for an apartment. He had found a tenant willing to sublet her apartment, but on one condition: she insisted that the new occupant buy the furniture she wanted to leave behind. On top of that, she was asking for a sum of money up front to finalize the sublease. So this man came to see me to ask whether such practices were legal.”
Après quelques recherches, Michel a déco: After doing some research, Michel discovered that this tenant had only one intention: to take advantage of the situation. “So I made it clear to him that these things were illegal.” But when it came to dishonest landlords, the public writer never hesitated to step in concretely, including by sending them letters directly. “I had a field day. I loved intimidating those crooked landlords!”
Chaque injustice est un moteur pour Mich: Every injustice drives Michel. “I get a rush of adrenaline when I see people being abused with impunity,” he confides, his fist clenched. “These people are under enormous pressure, especially when they have to prove they’ve found housing in order to move forward with their administrative procedures,” he lets drop.
Entre deux gorgées de <em>latte</em>, Mi: Between sips of latte, Michel also recalls a Haitian mother who came to see him after knocking on every door to assert her son’s rights. “This woman came to us through our organization’s pediatrician,” he says. The woman’s son had special needs, and she had been fighting for two years to have him transferred to a specialized school. “The principal of the school where her son was enrolled turned a deaf ear: no appointments granted, no answers to her requests. It was unbearable. We eventually understood that she was a victim of racism.”
Michel a alors senti une sainte colère m: Michel then felt a righteous anger rising in him. “I couldn’t understand how a school principal, who is supposed to stand up for children, would refuse to help a family with an urgent need,” he says, eyes wide. For him, it was no longer simply a matter of writing a letter or filling out a form. He launched into a veritable marathon of meetings. “Seven or eight appointments,” he specifies, tapping his pen on the page. Together, they wrote letters to the school board, filed complaints against the school and pushed for new meetings with the administration. In the end, the school board agreed to transfer the child to a school suited to his needs. “It was a victory!” Michel exclaims.
C’est à la lecture d’une lettre que la m: It was reading a letter the mother wrote to thank him that made him realize what this triumph meant. “It almost tore my heart out and brought tears to my eyes.” He pauses, seeming to relive the moment.
« Quand tu lis ces mots, quand tu vois c: “When you read those words, when you see what it meant to her, you realize that all that work, all those hours spent writing, making calls, is so much more than a simple administrative service. That’s the real reward of a public writer! It’s priceless!”
Il reprend, avant d’exploser de rire : «: He continues, before bursting into laughter: “But that’s why I take on every request... except love letters!”
<strong>Manque de fonds – écrivaine publ: Lack of funding: a public writer working from home
« Moi, ça m’est déjà arrivé, une fois, d: “It did happen to me once, I wrote a love letter,” says Suzanne Boivin, a language teacher for adults and a public writer who works from home.
Inspirée par Suzanne Coupal, une juge re: Inspired by Suzanne Coupal, a retired judge who became a public writer, Suzanne Boivin took the plunge in 2022. “It was what I was already doing naturally, helping people write documents. So I thought I could offer my services at a community centre.” After trying to work with an organization in Saint-Michel, a lack of funding forced her to work informally from her own home.
« Je n’ai pas beaucoup de temps, mais ce: “I don’t have a lot of time, but what I do have, I devote to my community.” In the residential neighbourhood where Suzanne lives, her neighbours don’t hesitate to ask for her help. “Often, people I’ve helped recommend me to others. I never say no, and word of mouth is very effective,” she says.
Grâce à sa formation juridique, Suzanne: Thanks to her legal training, Suzanne writes love letters as well as formal notices. “Sometimes I help people who need a letter to settle a dispute with their landlord. Or I’ve helped people who were being sued and couldn’t afford to defend themselves. I offered to help with the writing, explaining that if their case required legal representation, they would only have a lawyer’s fees to pay.”
Son soutien en tant qu’écrivaine publiqu: Her neighbours greatly value her support as a volunteer public writer. However, the lack of funding prevents her services from growing and reaching more people. “If public writers were hired directly and supported over the long term, people would feel more supported,” she adds. “Immigrants, in particular, are often very isolated and left to fend for themselves. There should be a resource they can truly count on.”
Benoît Gignac est écrivain public bénévo: Benoît Gignac has been a volunteer public writer at the Ahuntsic library since 2021. Photo: courtesy
Le réseau des bibliothèques de Montréal: For several years, the Montréal library network has collaborated with the Résidences d’écriture en bibliothèque program of the Union des écrivaines et des écrivains québécois, which has been suspended since 2023. The program allowed two libraries in the network to host a writer each year for a period of about six months. Despite the suspension of the program, some libraries are still offering a public writer service in their programming this fall, including in Anjou, Verdun and at the Ahuntsic library.
C’est justement dans un petit bureau de: It is in a small office at the Ahuntsic library that we meet Benoît Gignac, a volunteer public writer since 2021.
Bien que l’espace où nous nous trouvons: Although the space where we sit is empty, white and impersonal, the experience of being a public writer takes on a whole other dimension for Benoît. For him, every appointment is a new encounter that brings life to the place. “I see all kinds of people and requests, but very often they’re personal requests,” he explains.
À 69 ans, Benoît a un charisme naturel,: At 69, Benoît has a natural charisma, and his soothing voice immediately inspires trust. His eyes drift for a moment to the office’s bay window, and he smiles as he talks about a young girl he is helping to write poetry. “She makes quite a few mistakes in French, but her ideas are beautiful,” he says. Together, they go over words, explore nuances and look for the terms that best express her thoughts. “What I do is help them find their voice, express what’s on their heart, with the means they have.”
Le service qu’il propose est simple : le: The service he offers is simple: interested people book an appointment with the library, which then directs them to him. Before each meeting, Benoît takes the time to chat briefly with the person to make sure their needs match what he can offer.
Souvent, on le sollicite pour des demand: He is often asked for very specific help. “They’re generally women, and almost all of them are immigrants,” he explains. He recalls in particular a woman who was trying to pass a Ministry of Education exam to become a francization teacher. “She had failed twice because of time management. She was so focused on details that she never managed to finish on time. I simply told her: ‘You don’t have to write a perfect text, you just have to meet the deadline.’”
Son travail va bien au-delà de l’assista: His work goes well beyond writing assistance. He gives people tools to navigate complex situations. “I don’t teach the language,” he insists. “I help them overcome the concrete obstacles in front of them.”
La mission que Benoît s’est donnée s’app: The mission Benoît has set for himself is closer to that of a writing teacher than a public writer. Often, he doesn’t write for the people who come to him, but helps them write for themselves. “I work this way more often because these are people who come back often. These are projects I have with them.”
Même si certaines requêtes peuvent sembl: Even if some requests may seem less urgent, demand remains: “There are always people coming, so there must be a need… But I’ll admit I hesitated to accept your interview request because I don’t want this to become too well known – I’d risk being swamped!” he confides, laughing.
Alors que les services d’écrivain public: As public writer services become increasingly rare in the province, Benoît remains pragmatic. “I like what I do, and I do it my way. If others want to get involved, great, but I’m not going to make a crusade of it. That said, if someone starts a petition, I’ll sign it,” he says with an amused smile. It is not a personal fight, but a quiet contribution to the community. “I do my part, like all citizens my age should, whether it’s cleaning up the streets or delivering meals. In my case, I write, but I do what I can, within the limits of my abilities.”
La fin du projet pilote d’écrivains publ: The end of the public writer pilot project leaves a void for newcomers, who still face numerous administrative and language challenges in Quebec.
Le soutien de ces écrivains publics, bén: The support of these public writers, whether volunteer or paid, remains crucial to easing their integration. One question therefore arises: why abandon such an essential service when demand keeps growing?
Au moment d’écrire ces lignes, le minist: At the time of writing, the Ministry of the French Language had still not answered that question.
